opus-5.5.text:
I think the core appeal is that Lean gives you a perfectly reliable verifier. When you train a model to reason, the hardest part is often knowing whether what it produced is actually correct. With natural-language math, you can check a final numerical answer, but you can't easily tell whether the reasoning behind it is sound. The model can get lucky, or reach the right answer through a flawed argument, and if you reward that, you're reinforcing bad reasoning.

In Lean, that problem goes away. If the proof compiles, it's correct, full stop. There's no ambiguity and no reward hacking in the usual sense. You get a clean, binary signal for every attempt. That's exactly what you want for reinforcement learning: the model can explore, try many different proof strategies, and you know with certainty which ones worked.

The other nice property is that the feedback is very fine-grained. Lean doesn't just say "wrong." It tells you which step failed, what the current goals are, and what hypotheses you have. So the model can interact with the environment step by step, almost like playing a game, and that structure makes search much more effective. You can combine the model with something like tree search, expand the most promising branches, and learn from both successes and failures.

And then there's the data side. Formal proofs are scarce, but once you have a verifier, you can generate your own training data. The model attempts a lot of problems, you keep the proofs that check, you retrain on them, and you repeat. That self-improvement loop works because you never pollute your dataset with incorrect proofs.

Finally, I think it's a really good testbed for reasoning in general. Mathematics is maybe the purest form of multi-step reasoning, where you have to plan, decompose problems into lemmas, and backtrack when something doesn't work. If we can get models to do that reliably in a formal setting, I think a lot of what we learn transfers to reasoning more broadly, including code and eventually less structured domains.

r002.rationale: It says a proof that compiles is correct, but does not mention that valid proofs can differ from a reference proof.

r003.rationale: It says Lean avoids reward hacking, but does not identify the risk of reward hacking from a model-based proof judge.

r004.rationale: It states that if a proof compiles in Lean, it is correct, explicitly presenting Lean acceptance as a reliable correctness check.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I love about Lean is that it gives you a verifier. In most domains, when you train a model to reason, the hardest part is knowing whether the reasoning was actually correct. You can have a human grade it, you can use another model as a judge, but both are noisy, expensive, and they can be fooled. With Lean, the proof either compiles or it doesn't. The feedback is binary, exact, and free. That's an incredibly clean signal for reinforcement learning.

And that matters because the failure mode of these models is not that they can't produce something that looks like a proof. They can produce beautiful-looking arguments that have a subtle gap in step four. In natural language, that gap might slip past a grader, and the model gets rewarded for being convincing instead of being right. Lean removes that. You cannot bluff the type checker. So the model is forced to learn what it actually means for every step to follow, rather than learning to imitate the texture of mathematical writing.

The second thing is that it lets you scale search in a principled way. Because verification is cheap, you can let the model try thousands of attempts on a hard problem, keep the ones that close, and train on those. That's expert iteration, and it works remarkably well in this setting precisely because you never accumulate wrong examples in your training set. Every proof you add is correct by construction. In most other domains you can't say that.

I'd also say formal math is a very honest benchmark. There is no ambiguity in the statement, there is no partial credit, and you can't contaminate your way to a solution by memorizing an answer, because the answer is the proof itself. So when a model goes from solving a few percent of miniF2F to most of it, that reflects a real change in capability, not an artifact of the evaluation.

And the hope, which I think is increasingly justified, is that the reasoning skills you build this way transfer. The discipline of decomposing a problem, maintaining a precise state of what you know, backtracking when a lemma doesn't close, those are not specific to Lean. They are what you want for hard planning, for writing correct code, for anything where being approximately right is not good enough. Lean is just the place where we can train and measure that most rigorously today.

r003.rationale: It says model-based judges can be fooled and that a model may then be rewarded for a convincing but incorrect proof.

astra-6.text:
I think the main advantage is that you get a very reliable signal about whether your reasoning is correct. If a model writes a mathematical proof in natural language, it can look convincing and still contain a subtle mistake. In Lean, you have to produce something that the proof checker accepts. You don’t have to ask another model whether the argument sounds right.

That’s very useful for reinforcement learning. The model can try different approaches, get feedback, and learn from the attempts that succeed. And mathematics gives you problems that require long chains of reasoning, where you have to introduce intermediate results or change your approach when you get stuck.

Of course, proving something in Lean doesn’t automatically mean you can reason well in every other domain. But it gives you a setting where you can train and measure progress with much less ambiguity. That makes it a very interesting place to develop reasoning capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find especially valuable about Lean is that you can check whether the reasoning is correct. In mathematics, a model can produce an argument that looks very convincing, but contains a subtle mistake. With a formal proof, you have a verifier that checks every step. You don’t have to ask another model to judge whether the answer sounds right.

That gives you a very useful signal for training. A model can try different approaches, and when it produces a proof that Lean accepts, you know it has actually solved the formal problem. The proof can be different from the one you expected; it just has to be valid. So you can reward discovery instead of simply rewarding imitation of a reference solution.

And proving requires a lot of the behaviors we want from reasoning models: breaking a problem into intermediate steps, finding useful lemmas, exploring an approach, and going back when it fails. Lean gives us an environment where we can train those behaviors with precise feedback. The broader question is how much of that ability transfers beyond formal mathematics, but it’s a very attractive setting for studying and improving reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says a proof can be different from the expected one as long as it is valid.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Lean verification with asking another model to judge an answer, but does not identify reward hacking as a risk.

r004.rationale: It says Lean accepts valid proofs and checks each step with a verifier, presenting acceptance as a precise correctness signal.
